```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

```{r model-meta, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
mod <- readModelDb("Cha_2024_zolpidem")
ui <- rxode2::rxode(mod)
cat("* Citation: ", ui$reference, "\n", sep = "")
cat("* Article: <https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics16050689>\n")
cat("* Description: ", ui$description, "\n", sep = "")
```

Cha 2024 built a population PK model for oral zolpidem so that emergency
physicians could simulate plasma concentrations after an intentional overdose,
and wrapped it in a public web application. The data are the individual
plasma profiles of a single-dose 10 mg study in healthy Korean volunteers,
digitised from the figures of the regulatory study report. The final model is
one-compartment with first-order absorption after a lag time and first-order
elimination; sex was tested as a covariate and not retained.

The same 30-subject study (sampling 0-12 h, 15 per sex) is analysed from the
original concentrations, with a transit-absorption model and PD endpoints, in
`Kim_2026_zolpidem` (see that model's article). The two models are independent
fits and are not interchangeable: Cha 2024 used 23 digitised profiles and
reached a simpler structure.

# Population

```{r population, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
pop <- ui$meta$population
cat("* Species: ", pop$species, "\n", sep = "")
cat("* Subjects: ", pop$n_subjects, " (", pop$sex_female_pct, "% female)\n", sep = "")
cat("* Age (original 30 subjects): ", pop$age_mean, "\n", sep = "")
cat("* Weight (original 30 subjects): ", pop$weight_mean, "\n", sep = "")
cat("* Disease state: ", pop$disease_state, "\n", sep = "")
cat("* Dose: ", pop$dose_range, "\n", sep = "")
cat("* Region: ", pop$regions, "\n", sep = "")
```

Seven of the 30 subjects in the regulatory report were dropped because their
plotted profiles duplicated other subjects' plots, leaving 12 males and 11
females (Results 3.1). Individual demographics could not be recovered, so the
age and weight above are those of the full original study; sex was the only
covariate the authors could test.

## Encoded variances against the printed CV%

Each IIV row of Table 2 is printed as a CV%. The model encodes
`omega^2 = log(1 + CV^2)`; the next section shows why. This block recovers the
printed CV% and correlation from the encoded matrix, row by row.

```{r omega-roundtrip}
om <- ui$omega
printed_cv <- c(etalka = 158.91, etalcl = 32.60, etalvc = 22.10)
recovered_cv <- 100 * sqrt(exp(diag(om)[names(printed_cv)]) - 1)
recovered_rho <- om["etalcl", "etalvc"] / sqrt(om["etalcl", "etalcl"] * om["etalvc", "etalvc"])
data.frame(
  eta = c(names(printed_cv), "rho(CL, Vd)"),
  printed = c(printed_cv, 0.853),
  recovered = signif(c(recovered_cv, recovered_rho), 4)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Table 2 IIV rows recovered from the encoded omega matrix.")
# Rounding of the encoded variances to 3-4 significant figures moves the CV
# by at most ~0.1 point and the correlation by ~0.001.
stopifnot(
  max(abs(recovered_cv - printed_cv)) < 0.2,
  abs(recovered_rho - 0.853) < 0.002
)
```

# Which scale did Table 2 use?

## IIV: log(1 + CV^2), not omega x 100

Table 2 labels each IIV row `omega2 <parameter> (CV%)`. On the narrow rows
(CL 32.6%, Vd 22.1%) the two common conventions, `CV% = 100 * omega` and
`CV% = 100 * sqrt(exp(omega^2) - 1)`, give nearly the same variance, but on
the Ka row (158.9%) they differ two-fold: 2.53 versus 1.26. A third reading,
that the printed number is `100 * omega^2`, would put the CL CV at 60%, which
the digitised NCA rules out (Table 1 CL/F SD is 32% and 28% of the mean in
males and females).

The paper's own Monte Carlo summary settles it. Table 3 reports, for 500
simulated subjects per dose and no residual error (the Figure 5 profiles are
smooth), how long each subject stays above the toxic, comatose and fatal
thresholds. The closed-form one-compartment solution below repeats that
calculation for 4000 subjects per dose under each reading. Base R's random
number generator is used so that the numbers are identical on every machine.

```{r scale-check}
closed_form_cohort <- function(dose_mg, omega2, n = 4000, dt = 0.02, seed = 20240520) {
  set.seed(seed)
  z1 <- rnorm(n)
  z2 <- rnorm(n)
  zka <- rnorm(n)
  # Correlated (CL, Vd) etas with rho = 0.853 (Table 2).
  eta_cl <- sqrt(omega2[["cl"]]) * z1
  eta_vc <- sqrt(omega2[["vc"]]) * (0.853 * z1 + sqrt(1 - 0.853^2) * z2)
  ka <- 5.41 * exp(sqrt(omega2[["ka"]]) * zka)
  cl <- 16.9 * exp(eta_cl)
  vc <- 61.7 * exp(eta_vc)
  k <- cl / vc
  tt <- seq(0, 24, by = dt)
  td <- pmax(outer(rep(1, n), tt) - 0.394, 0)
  conc <- 1000 * dose_mg / vc * ka / (ka - k) * (exp(-k * td) - exp(-ka * td))
  list(conc = conc, dt = dt)
}
time_above_category <- function(cohort, threshold) {
  dur <- rowSums(cohort$conc > threshold) * cohort$dt
  cut(dur, c(-Inf, 0, 1, 2, 3, Inf), labels = c("NR", "<1 h", "1-2 h", "2-3 h", ">3 h"))
}
cv <- c(ka = 1.5891, cl = 0.326, vc = 0.221)
readings <- list(
  "log(1 + CV^2) (encoded)" = log(1 + cv^2),
  "omega x 100" = cv^2,
  "omega^2 x 100" = cv
)
scale_tab <- lapply(names(readings), function(r) {
  c280 <- closed_form_cohort(280, readings[[r]])
  c560 <- closed_form_cohort(560, readings[[r]])
  data.frame(
    reading = r,
    `comatose NR, 280 mg` = 100 * mean(time_above_category(c280, 1500) == "NR"),
    `fatal >3 h, 280 mg` = 100 * mean(time_above_category(c280, 4000) == ">3 h"),
    `fatal NR, 560 mg` = 100 * mean(time_above_category(c560, 4000) == "NR"),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows()
scale_tab <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(reading = "Cha 2024 Table 3 (N = 500)", `comatose NR, 280 mg` = 0.2,
             `fatal >3 h, 280 mg` = 0.2, `fatal NR, 560 mg` = 2.6, check.names = FALSE),
  scale_tab
)
knitr::kable(scale_tab, digits = 1,
             caption = "Percent of subjects in three Table 3 cells under each reading of the IIV scale (4000 subjects per dose).")
```

```{r scale-gate}
paper <- unlist(scale_tab[1, -1])
dev <- sapply(2:4, function(i) max(abs(unlist(scale_tab[i, -1]) - paper)))
names(dev) <- scale_tab$reading[2:4]
dev
# Realised: 0.55 points for log(1 + CV^2), 4.0 for omega x 100 and 8.9 for
# omega^2 x 100. A binomial SE at N = 500 is at most 0.7 points for these cells,
# so only the encoded reading is within sampling error of the paper. Base R's
# generator makes these numbers the same on every machine.
stopifnot(dev[[1]] < 1.5, dev[[2]] > 2.5, dev[[3]] > 2.5)
```

## Residual error: 0.284 is an SD

Table 2 prints `Proportional error 0.284` without saying whether it is the SD
or the variance of `eps_prop`. The two readings give a 28% and a 53%
proportional error. Residual noise on the 6, 8 and 12 h samples feeds straight
into the terminal-slope estimate, so the between-subject spread of NCA
lambda-z on the study design discriminates them: the digitised Table 1 SDs
are 0.06 1/h (males) and 0.04 1/h (females).

```{r study-design}
study_times <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12)
n_study <- 200
ev_study <- rxode2::et(amt = 10, cmt = "depot") |>
  rxode2::et(study_times, cmt = "central") |>
  rxode2::et(id = seq_len(n_study))

rxode2::rxSetSeed(2024)
sim_obs <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = ev_study, returnType = "data.frame")
rxode2::rxSetSeed(2024)
sim_obs_var <- rxode2::rxSolve(ui |> rxode2::ini(propSd = sqrt(0.284)),
                               events = ev_study, returnType = "data.frame")
```

```{r nca-functions}
run_nca <- function(sim, conc_col, dose_ug = 10000) {
  conc <- sim |>
    dplyr::transmute(id, time, conc = .data[[conc_col]], treatment = "10 mg") |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(conc)) |>
    # A proportional residual of 53% leaves a few samples below zero; an
    # observed concentration cannot be negative, so floor them as BLQ.
    dplyr::mutate(conc = pmax(conc, 0))
  # Dose in ug so that ug / (ng*h/mL) gives CL/F in L/h and Vz/F in L.
  dose <- data.frame(id = seq_len(max(conc$id)), time = 0, dose = dose_ug, treatment = "10 mg")
  o_conc <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc, conc ~ time | treatment + id)
  o_dose <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose, dose ~ time | treatment + id)
  intervals <- data.frame(
    start = c(0, 0), end = c(12, Inf),
    auclast = c(TRUE, FALSE),
    cmax = c(FALSE, TRUE), tmax = c(FALSE, TRUE),
    lambda.z = c(FALSE, TRUE), half.life = c(FALSE, TRUE),
    cl.obs = c(FALSE, TRUE), vz.obs = c(FALSE, TRUE)
  )
  PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, intervals = intervals))
}
nca_sd <- run_nca(sim_obs, "sim")
nca_var <- run_nca(sim_obs_var, "sim")
lz_sd <- function(res) {
  r <- as.data.frame(res)
  sd(r$PPORRES[r$PPTESTCD == "lambda.z"], na.rm = TRUE)
}
ruv_tab <- data.frame(
  reading = c("Table 1 digitised, males", "Table 1 digitised, females",
              "propSd = 0.284 (encoded)", "propSd = sqrt(0.284) = 0.533"),
  `SD of lambda-z (1/h)` = c(0.06, 0.04, lz_sd(nca_sd), lz_sd(nca_var)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(ruv_tab, digits = 3, caption = "Between-subject SD of NCA lambda-z, study design, 10 mg.")
```

```{r ruv-gate}
# The two solves share the seed, so their etas and standardised residuals are
# paired and the ratio is far steadier than either SD. Over seeds 1-6 the SD
# reading gave 0.067-0.086 1/h, the variance reading 0.114-0.138 1/h, and the
# ratio 1.36-1.90.
stopifnot(ruv_tab[[2]][3] < 0.10, ruv_tab[[2]][4] / ruv_tab[[2]][3] > 1.2)
```

The variance reading raises the lambda-z spread by about half again, further
from the digitised data; the SD reading is closer to it. Part of the remaining excess
under the SD reading comes from the 23 digitised subjects being fewer and
smoother than a simulated cohort, so the comparison is directional, not exact.

# Non-compartmental analysis against Table 1

Table 1 reports NCA of the digitised data by sex. The model has no sex
effect, so the reference below is the subject-weighted mean of the two
digitised columns (12 males, 11 females). Simulated values are the cohort
**means** of the per-subject NCA on the study sampling design, with residual
error, which is what the digitised NCA measured.

```{r nca-compare}
nca_df <- as.data.frame(nca_sd)
sim_mean <- nca_df |>
  dplyr::filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "auclast", "cl.obs", "half.life", "vz.obs")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(PPTESTCD) |>
  dplyr::summarise(PPORRES = mean(PPORRES, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
w <- c(12, 11) / 23
reference <- data.frame(
  cmax = sum(w * c(162.72, 189.22)),
  auclast = sum(w * c(542.5, 688.1)),
  cl.obs = sum(w * c(18.88, 14.93)),
  half.life = sum(w * c(3.58, 3.02)),
  vz.obs = sum(w * c(92.2, 63.5))
)
cmp_nca <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = sim_mean,
  reference = reference,
  units = c(cmax = "ng/mL", auclast = "ng*h/mL", cl.obs = "L/h", half.life = "h", vz.obs = "L"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(cmp_nca, caption = "Simulated (cohort mean, 200 subjects) vs. Cha 2024 Table 1 digitised NCA (subject-weighted mean of the male and female columns). AUC is AUC0-12h. * differs by >20%.")
attr(cmp_nca, "footnote")
```

```{r nca-gate}
pd <- setNames(as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9.+-]", "", cmp_nca$`% diff`)), cmp_nca[[1]])
pd
# Cmax, AUC0-12 and CL/F are the exposure metrics the model must carry; with a
# between-subject CV of ~30-35% the cohort-mean SE at 200 subjects is ~2.5%,
# so 20% still breaks on a mis-transcribed CL, V or dose unit. Half-life and
# Vz/F are reported, not gated: see the deviation below.
stopifnot(all(abs(pd[grepl("Cmax|AUC|CL", names(pd))]) < 20))
```

The exposure metrics agree. The terminal half-life does not: the model's
typical elimination rate constant is 16.9 / 61.7 = 0.274 1/h (half-life
2.5 h), while the digitised data give a mean terminal half-life of 3.3 h, and
Vz/F (= CL/F / lambda-z) runs low for the same reason. The one-compartment fit is
driven by the high concentrations around the peak; the slower late phase that
NCA sees on the 8-12 h samples is what the original-study analysis described
with a second compartment, and it matches the "slight underprediction" the
authors note in their VPC (Figure 3). The model is used as published.

# Replicating the figures

## Figure 3: visual predictive check, 10 mg

```{r fig3, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 3 of Cha 2024: 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles of simulated observations (with residual error) after a single 10 mg dose, 200 subjects."}
sim_obs |>
  dplyr::group_by(time) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    p05 = quantile(sim, 0.05), p50 = quantile(sim, 0.5), p95 = quantile(sim, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(time)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p05, ymax = p95), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = p50), colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(aes(y = p05), colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = p95), colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Time after dose (h)", y = "Zolpidem concentration (ng/mL)") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Figure 5 and Table 3: overdose simulations

Figure 5 and Table 3 simulate single oral doses of 10, 280, 560 and 1120 mg
(one tablet, and one, two and four 28-tablet packages) without residual
error. The paper used 500 subjects per dose; 200 are used here.

```{r overdose-sim}
doses <- c(10, 280, 560, 1120)
n_arm <- 200
grid <- seq(0, 24, by = 0.05)
ev_od <- lapply(seq_along(doses), function(i) {
  rxode2::et(amt = doses[[i]], cmt = "depot") |>
    rxode2::et(grid, cmt = "central") |>
    rxode2::et(id = (i - 1) * n_arm + seq_len(n_arm)) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    dplyr::mutate(dose_mg = doses[[i]])
}) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows()
rxode2::rxSetSeed(560)
sim_od <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = ev_od, keep = "dose_mg", returnType = "data.frame")
```

```{r fig5, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 5 of Cha 2024: individual simulated profiles; yellow, orange and red lines mark the toxic (500), comatose (1500) and fatal (4000 ng/mL) thresholds."}
thr <- data.frame(y = c(500, 1500, 4000), level = c("toxic", "comatose", "fatal"))
ggplot(sim_od, aes(time, Cc, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_hline(data = thr, aes(yintercept = y, colour = level)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(toxic = "gold", comatose = "orange", fatal = "red")) +
  facet_wrap(~ paste(dose_mg, "mg"), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Zolpidem concentration (ng/mL)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

Table 3 counts, per subject, the time the concentration stays above each
threshold. Its "toxic" row is 100% "> 3 h" at every overdose; the time spent
*within* the 500-1500 ng/mL band would put a few percent of the 280 mg
subjects in the 2-3 h category, so the rows are read as cumulative time
above 500, 1500 and 4000 ng/mL.

```{r table3}
dt <- 0.05
dur_tab <- sim_od |>
  dplyr::group_by(dose_mg, id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    toxic = sum(Cc > 500) * dt, comatose = sum(Cc > 1500) * dt, fatal = sum(Cc > 4000) * dt,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(toxic, comatose, fatal), names_to = "level", values_to = "dur") |>
  dplyr::mutate(cat = cut(dur, c(-Inf, 0, 1, 2, 3, Inf), labels = c("NR", "<1 h", "1-2 h", "2-3 h", ">3 h"))) |>
  dplyr::count(level, dose_mg, cat, .drop = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::group_by(level, dose_mg) |>
  dplyr::mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

paper_t3 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~level, ~dose_mg, ~NR, ~`<1 h`, ~`1-2 h`, ~`2-3 h`, ~`>3 h`,
  "toxic", 10, 100, 0, 0, 0, 0,
  "toxic", 280, 0, 0, 0, 0, 100,
  "toxic", 560, 0, 0, 0, 0, 100,
  "toxic", 1120, 0, 0, 0, 0, 100,
  "comatose", 10, 100, 0, 0, 0, 0,
  "comatose", 280, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 15.0, 83.6,
  "comatose", 560, 0, 0, 0, 0.4, 99.6,
  "comatose", 1120, 0, 0, 0, 0, 100,
  "fatal", 10, 100, 0, 0, 0, 0,
  "fatal", 280, 58.8, 21.4, 15.6, 4.0, 0.2,
  "fatal", 560, 2.6, 1.6, 11.2, 31.4, 53.2,
  "fatal", 1120, 0, 0, 0, 1.6, 98.4
) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-c(level, dose_mg), names_to = "cat", values_to = "paper")

t3 <- dur_tab |>
  dplyr::mutate(cat = as.character(cat)) |>
  dplyr::left_join(paper_t3, by = c("level", "dose_mg", "cat"))
stopifnot(nrow(t3) == 60, !anyNA(t3$paper))

t3 |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", pct, paper)) |>
  dplyr::select(level, dose_mg, cat, cell) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = cat, values_from = cell) |>
  dplyr::mutate(level = factor(level, c("toxic", "comatose", "fatal"))) |>
  dplyr::arrange(level, dose_mg) |>
  dplyr::rename(Threshold = level, `Dose (mg)` = dose_mg) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Percent of subjects by time above each threshold: simulated, 200 per dose (Cha 2024 Table 3, 500 per dose, in parentheses).")
```

```{r table3-gate}
# Model-true cell values (4000-subject closed form above): fatal NR at 280 mg
# ~60%, fatal >3 h at 560 mg ~52%. The binomial SE at 200 subjects is <= 3.6
# points, so 15 points is > 4 SE yet still breaks on a mis-transcribed CL, V
# or ka, each of which moves these cells by tens of points.
cell <- function(lv, d, ct) {
  v <- t3$pct[t3$level == lv & t3$dose_mg == d & t3$cat == ct]
  if (length(v) != 1L) stop("no unique cell for ", lv, " ", d, " ", ct)
  v
}
stopifnot(
  abs(cell("fatal", 280, "NR") - 58.8) < 15,
  abs(cell("fatal", 560, ">3 h") - 53.2) < 15,
  cell("fatal", 1120, ">3 h") > 85,
  cell("comatose", 560, ">3 h") > 90,
  # A 10 mg dose stays below the toxic threshold (model 95th-percentile Cmax
  # ~200 ng/mL); a tolerance, not exact zero.
  cell("toxic", 10, "NR") > 98
)
```

## Figure 4: the web application's 200 mg example

```{r fig4, fig.cap = "Replicates the simulation plot of Figure 4 of Cha 2024: 200 mg (twenty 10 mg tablets), median and 5th-95th percentile band of 200 simulated subjects."}
ev_200 <- rxode2::et(amt = 200, cmt = "depot") |>
  rxode2::et(grid, cmt = "central") |>
  rxode2::et(id = seq_len(n_arm))
rxode2::rxSetSeed(200)
sim_200 <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = ev_200, returnType = "data.frame")
band_200 <- sim_200 |>
  dplyr::group_by(time) |>
  dplyr::summarise(p05 = quantile(Cc, 0.05), p50 = median(Cc), p95 = quantile(Cc, 0.95), .groups = "drop")
ggplot(band_200, aes(time)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p05, ymax = p95), fill = "lightblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = p50), colour = "steelblue4") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(200, 500, 1500, 4000), colour = c("grey50", "gold", "orange", "red")) +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Zolpidem concentration (ng/mL)") +
  theme_bw()
```

The application's panel reports a median concentration peaking near
2500 ng/mL with a 95th percentile just under 4000 ng/mL and a typical
elimination rate constant of 0.27 1/h; the simulation above has the same
shape and scale.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **IIV scale.** Table 2 prints the IIV rows as CV%. They are encoded as
  `omega^2 = log(1 + CV^2)`, the reading that reproduces the paper's Table 3
  Monte Carlo summary; `CV% = 100 * omega` would give twice the Ka variance and
  is inconsistent with Table 3 (see "Which scale did Table 2 use?").
* **Residual-error scale.** `Proportional error 0.284` is encoded as the SD of
  the proportional error; the variance reading would widen the simulated
  spread of the terminal slope beyond the digitised data.
* **Vd-CL correlation.** Printed as a correlation (rho = 0.853) and converted
  to the covariance with the encoded variances.
* **Terminal half-life.** The model's half-life (2.5 h typical) is shorter than
  the digitised NCA half-life (3.3 h); the model is used as published and this
  is not adjusted (see the NCA section).
* **Table 3 thresholds.** Read as cumulative time above 500, 1500 and
  4000 ng/mL, the reading consistent with the printed 100% "> 3 h" toxic rows.
* **Source data.** The model was fitted to concentrations digitised from
  figures, not to the original measurements; the authors show the digitised
  NCA matches the original NCA (Table 1). No errata were found for the article
  (checked 2026-10-30).
* **Dose in overdose.** As the authors note, absorption after dozens of tablets
  may be slower or less complete than after one; the model carries the
  single-tablet absorption to all doses, as the paper's simulations do.
